name: Fourth Lateran Council
also_known_as: Lateran IV; twelfth ecumenical council (Catholic count)
summary: Pope Innocent III's great reforming council, which first officially used the word 'transubstantiation', required yearly confession, organized the suppression of heresy, and imposed distinctive dress on Jews and Muslims.

background.text: Innocent III summoned the council in 1213 to reform the church, fight heresy (especially the Cathars of southern France, already the target of the Albigensian Crusade), and launch a new crusade.

happened.text: About 400 bishops and 800 abbots and priors attended, with envoys of kings and the Eastern Latin patriarchs, making it the largest council of the Middle Ages; it issued 71 constitutions in three sessions.

Canon 1 set out a profession of faith declaring that there is one universal church 'outside which no one at all is saved', and that in the Eucharist the bread and wine are 'transubstantiated' into Christ's body and blood.
Canon 21 (Omnis utriusque sexus) required every Catholic who had reached the age of discretion to confess to their own priest and receive Communion at least once a year, at Easter.

Canon 3 required secular rulers to expel heretics from their lands on pain of excommunication and loss of their territory, and gave those who fought heretics the same indulgence as crusaders to the Holy Land.

Canons 68 and 69 required Jews and Muslims ('Saracens') to wear clothing that distinguished them from Christians, forbade Jews to appear in public during Holy Week, and barred them from public office.
Canon 18 forbade clergy to bless judicial ordeals, which helped end trial by ordeal in Western Europe.
The council planned a new crusade (the Fifth Crusade, launched 1217), confirmed Frederick II as emperor, and handed most lands of Count Raymond VI of Toulouse to the crusade leader Simon de Montfort.

participants.name: Innocent III
participants.role: Pope who called and led the council

participants.name: Raymond VI of Toulouse
participants.role: Count whose lands were given to Simon de Montfort for failing to suppress the Cathars

outcomes.text: Its canons on confession, preaching, and clerical life shaped Catholic parish practice for centuries, and its profession of faith made transubstantiation the official term for the Eucharist.
The dress rules led to compulsory badges for Jews in England (1218), France, and elsewhere; historians see the council as a turning point in the legal segregation of Jews in Christian Europe.
Its framework for suppressing heresy fed into the inquisitions established in the 1230s.

condemnations.reason: Joachim of Fiore's treatise on the Trinity, attacking Peter Lombard, condemned (Joachim himself, who had died in 1202, was declared a Catholic)
The teaching of Amalric of Bena (d. c. 1206) condemned as insane
Cathars, Waldensians, and all heretics excommunicated and anathematized (canon 3)

persecution_note: The council's decrees set rules that later bodies enforced. It named no individual for punishment but laid down how heretics and religious minorities were to be treated.

persecution.title: Measures against heretics
persecution.summary: Canon 3 ordered that condemned heretics be handed to the secular power for punishment, that suspects who could not prove their innocence be excommunicated, and that rulers who failed to purge heretics lose their lands to Catholics who would.

responsible.name: Innocent III and the Fourth Lateran Council
Secular rulers enforcing it
responsible.jurisdiction: Kingdoms and lordships of Latin Christendom

persecution.outcome: Basis for later inquisitions and crusades against heretics.

persecution.title: Distinctive dress and restrictions for Jews and Muslims
persecution.summary: Canons 68–69 required Jews and Muslims to dress differently from Christians, kept Jews off the streets in Holy Week, and barred them from public office; canon 67 restricted Jewish moneylending.

responsible.name: Innocent III and the Fourth Lateran Council
Kings and bishops who enforced badges
responsible.role: Applied the rules, for example in England from 1218

persecution.outcome: Badges and dress rules for Jews spread across Europe.
